Results show that combination therapy (IV alteplase + thrombectomy) improved functional outcomes in patients without admission hyperglycemia (acOR 1.46, 95% CI 1.04–2.07; absolute +6% mRS 0–1, aOR 1.71) but performed worse in hyperglycemic patients (acOR 0.74, 95% CI 0.46–1.20; and a significant 12.3% absolute decrease in excellent outcome, aOR 0.42, 95% CI 0.19–0.95). These findings indicate that baseline glucose modifies the clinical effect of alteplase, consistent with the proposed mechanism that hyperglycemia can worsen outcomes (plausibly via increased hemorrhagic risk/endothelial vulnerability) when alteplase is given. However, this is a post-hoc subgroup analysis in a specific large-vessel-occlusion population and the abstract does not report hemorrhage rates or direct biological measures, so while the clinical pattern supports the mechanism, causality and generalizability remain uncertain.

abstracts_analyzed.title: Effect of Admission Hyperglycemia on Safety and Efficacy of Intravenous Alteplase Before Thrombectomy in Ischemic Stroke: Post-hoc Analysis of the DIRECT-MT trial.

Therefore the data show that baseline glucose (via SHR1) is a prognostic predictor of worse outcomes after thrombolysed stroke, but do not demonstrate that baseline glucose modifies the magnitude of treatment benefit or specifically mediates increased harm from alteplase compared to control. The findings are consistent with the proposed biological mechanism (higher glucose linked to more hemorrhagic complications), but they do not provide evidence of treatment-by-glucose interaction.

abstracts_analyzed.reasoning: The abstract explicitly evaluates intravenous alteplase as part of 'bridging therapy' versus direct EVT and directly analyzes baseline glucose. It reports that higher baseline glucose was associated with greater odds of hemorrhagic transformation overall (adjusted OR 1.168 per 1 mmol/L) and—crucially—describes a statistically significant treatment-by-glucose interaction: at glucose >11.1 mmol/L bridging (alteplase+EVT) carried substantially higher risk of parenchymal hematoma than direct EVT (OR 4.84, p=0.024). This matches the proposed mechanism (glucose-related vulnerability to hemorrhage after thrombolysis) by showing a differential harm of alteplase in the high-glucose subgroup. Confidence is tempered because the analysis is post hoc, subgroup size is small (n=71 for >11.1 mmol/L), and the report focuses on hemorrhagic outcomes rather than functional endpoints, limiting clinical generalizability.
